items: Interpret a realistic Request for Proposal (RFP) and translate business goals into an architecture vision.
Produce Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) that justify trade-offs with evidence.
Design a logical and physical target architecture using cloud-native, event-driven, multi-region patterns.
Define a pragmatic migration strategy (7R / Strangler Fig) that de-risks legacy modernization.
Document a complete Software Architecture Document (SAD) and present it convincingly to stakeholders.
Self-assess against an evaluation rubric covering completeness, soundness, clarity, and communication.
RFP (Request for Proposal) — a client document inviting vendors/architects to propose a solution to a stated business problem.
SAD (Software Architecture Document) — the formal deliverable describing the architecture, rationale, and constraints.
ADR (Architecture Decision Record) — a short, immutable record of an important architectural decision, its context, and consequences.
7R — the seven cloud migration strategies: Rehost, Replatform, Refactor, Repurchase, Retain, Retire, Relocate.
Strangler Fig Pattern — incrementally replacing legacy functionality with new services behind a façade until the old system is "strangled."
NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) — quality attributes such as scalability, availability, security, and latency.
Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) — components communicate through events, enabling loose coupling and real-time reactions.
Multi-Region — running workloads across multiple geographic regions for resilience, latency, and compliance.

blocks.text: This is the capstone of the Solution Architect Academy. Working individually or in teams of 2–4, you step into the role of a Solution Architect responding to a client RFP. Your goal is to deliver a convincing, technically sound proposal and, most importantly, a complete Software Architecture Document (SAD) that a delivery team could actually execute.

The exercise mirrors real engagements: ambiguous requirements, conflicting stakeholders, budget ceilings, and legacy debt. You are graded not on building the system, but on architecting it — making defensible decisions, documenting them, and communicating the trade-offs.
Client: Northwind Retail Group (NRG) — a mid-size retailer (≈1,200 employees, €180M annual revenue) operating in the EU and UK.

items: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) — at least 6 ADRs for pivotal choices (cloud provider, decomposition strategy, data stores, event backbone, AI approach, multi-region topology). Each ADR must state context, decision, alternatives considered, and consequences.
Logical & Physical Architecture — with diagrams. Logical: domains, bounded contexts, data flows. Physical: concrete services, clusters, regions, networks.
Migration Plan — map each legacy component to one of the 7R strategies; sequence using the Strangler Fig pattern; define cutover and rollback.
Resilience & Data Strategy — failure modes, circuit breakers, bulkheads, idempotency; data partitioning, replication, consistency, GDPR handling.
Cost & Risk Assessment — TCO model, savings thesis, top-10 risks with likelihood/impact/mitigation.
The SAD Document — the integrated deliverable (structure below) that ties 1–5 together.

blocks.text: Use the arc42-inspired structure below. Every section must be present, even if brief.

items: Introduction & Goals — context, stakeholders, success metrics.
Constraints — technical, organizational, legal (GDPR/PCI), budget.
Context & Scope — system boundary, external actors, current vs. target.
Solution Strategy — the big architectural ideas and patterns.
Building Blocks (Logical) — bounded contexts, modules, interfaces.
Runtime/Physical View — deployment, regions, nodes, containers.
Data View — stores, flows, ownership, retention.
Cross-Cutting Concepts — security, logging, config, CI/CD.
Architecture Decisions (ADRs) — numbered records.
Migration & Roadmap — 7R mapping, Strangler phases, milestones.
Quality/Resilience & NFR Mapping — how each NFR is met.
Risks & Costs — risk register, TCO.
Glossary.

rows: All 13 SAD sections + 6 ADRs present and coherent.
Decisions justified with alternatives, evidence, and honest consequences.
Mermaid/C4 diagrams are readable, correctly labeled, and consistent.
Every stated NFR (avail, latency, security, DR) has a concrete mechanism.
Conflicts (cost vs. resilience, speed vs. quality) are surfaced and resolved.
SAD reads like a professional proposal; pitch is clear and persuasive.

items: Weeks 1–2: RFP analysis, stakeholders, baseline ADR 000 (provider/strategy).
Weeks 3–5: Logical architecture, domain decomposition, ADRs 001–003.
Weeks 6–8: Physical architecture, data & resilience strategy, ADRs 004–006.
Weeks 9–12: Strangler migration plan, first legacy module cutover (read-only path).
Weeks 13–18: AI assistant spike, multi-region topology, DR drills.
Weeks 19–24: Cost/risk model, SAD integration, stakeholder review & pitch.
Weeks 25–36: Incremental delivery aligned to SAD; monthly demos.

blocks.text: See the rubric table in the Explanation section. Final grade = weighted sum, with a hard gate: a submission missing any of the six required deliverables (ADRs, logical/physical architecture, migration plan, resilience & data strategy, cost & risk, SAD) cannot score above "Incomplete" regardless of other quality.

items: A (90–100): All dimensions strong; ADRs show real engineering judgment; diagrams unambiguous; NFRs fully traced.
B (75–89): Complete and sound, minor gaps in trade-off depth or NFR tracing.
C (60–74): Present but shallow; weak consequences or missing diagram clarity.
D (<60): Incomplete or technically unsound; NFRs unaddressed.
